steps.text: The derivative measures how fast a function changes: the slope of a graph, the velocity of a vehicle, the growth rate of a population. At school you practised differentiation rules. At university the "why" is added – this chapter refreshes both and prepares you for formal differential calculus.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. From the secant to the tangent
2. Differentiation rules: power, sum, product, quotient, chain
3. Curve sketching: monotonicity, extrema, curvature, inflection points
4. Optimisation problems
steps.section: Chapter 1 · The idea of the derivative
steps.insight: The derivative \(f'(a)\) is the slope of the tangent to the graph at the point \((a, f(a))\) – the best linear approximation of \(f\) near \(a\).

steps.text: The slope of a line through two points of the graph is called the difference quotient. If you let the second point approach the first, you get the tangent.
steps.explanation:
The animation does this for \(f(x) = x^2\) at \(a = 1\): the secant through \(P = (1, 1)\) and a point to its right tips into the tangent as the distance \(h\) tends to \(0\).

Calculation: \(\frac{(1 + h)^2 - 1}{h} = \frac{2h + h^2}{h} = 2 + h \to 2\). So \(f'(1) = 2\).

The limit does not always exist: \(f(x) = |x|\) has a corner at \(0\), where the function is not differentiable. You will learn more in "Differential Calculus".
steps.section: Chapter 1 · The idea of the derivative
steps.insight: Difference quotient = average slope (secant), differential quotient = instantaneous slope (tangent).

steps.text: If you assign each point \(x\) its slope, you get the derivative function \(f'\). With the derivative you can set up the tangent:
steps.formula: f(x) = x^2: \quad f'(x) = 2x; \qquad \text{tangent at } a: \quad y = f(a) + f'(a)\,(x - a)
steps.explanation:
Example: tangent to \(x^2\) at \(a = 1\): \(y = 1 + 2(x - 1) = 2x - 1\).

At \(a = 3\) with \(f(x) = x^2 - 4x\): \(f'(x) = 2x - 4\), so \(f'(3) = 2\) and \(f(3) = -3\). Tangent: \(y = -3 + 2(x - 3) = 2x - 9\).

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent: its slope is \(-\frac{1}{f'(a)}\).

A horizontal tangent means \(f'(a) = 0\) – important for extrema.
steps.section: Chapter 1 · The idea of the derivative
steps.insight: Tangent equation = point-slope form: through the point \((a, f(a))\) with slope \(f'(a)\).

steps.text: You don't have to compute the limit every time. The most important functions have known derivatives:
steps.formula:
\begin{array}{c|c}
f(x) & f'(x) \\ \hline
c & 0 \\
x^n & n\,x^{n-1} \\
\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} & \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\
\dfrac{1}{x} = x^{-1} & -\dfrac{1}{x^2} \\
e^x & e^x \\
\ln x & \dfrac{1}{x} \\
\sin x & \cos x \\
\cos x & -\sin x
\end{array}
steps.explanation:
The power rule holds for every exponent \(n \in \mathbb{R}\). That's why you first rewrite roots and fractions as powers: \(\sqrt[3]{x} = x^{1/3}\), \(\frac{1}{x^2} = x^{-2}\).

Examples:
• \((x^5)' = 5x^4\)
• \(\left(\frac{1}{x^2}\right)' = (x^{-2})' = -2x^{-3} = -\frac{2}{x^3}\)
• \((\sqrt{x})' = \frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\)
steps.insight: Remember: the cosine has the minus in its derivative: \((\cos x)' = -\sin x\) – sign mistake no. 1 with trigonometric derivatives.

steps.text: Sums and constant factors may be differentiated term by term:
steps.explanation:
Each summand is differentiated separately, constants as factors stay, constants as summands vanish (\(-7\) becomes \(0\)).

Example with standard functions: \((2\sin x + 3e^x - \ln x)' = 2\cos x + 3e^x - \frac{1}{x}\).

Careful: this does NOT hold for products and quotients. \((x \cdot e^x)' \neq 1 \cdot e^x\).
steps.insight: The derivative is linear: \((af + bg)' = af' + bg'\). That is why polynomials are so easy to differentiate.

steps.text: The product rule for \(f(x) = u(x) \cdot v(x)\):
steps.explanation:
Example: \(f(x) = x^2 e^x\) with \(u = x^2\), \(v = e^x\):
\(f'(x) = 2x \cdot e^x + x^2 \cdot e^x = e^x(2x + x^2)\).

Intuition: a rectangle with sides \(u\) and \(v\) grows on both sides at once. The increase consists of two strips: \(u'v\) and \(uv'\).

The most common mistake: \((uv)' = u'v'\). Counter-check: \((x \cdot x)' = (x^2)' = 2x\), but \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\).
steps.insight: Use the product rule when two factors both depend on \(x\). For a constant factor the factor rule suffices.

steps.explanation:
Example: \(f(x) = \frac{x}{x^2 + 1}\) with \(u = x\), \(v = x^2 + 1\):
\(f'(x) = \frac{1 \cdot (x^2 + 1) - x \cdot 2x}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \frac{1 - x^2}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\).

Memory aid: "low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared".

Often you can simplify the fraction first and save the quotient rule: \(\frac{x^2 + 1}{x} = x + \frac{1}{x}\) has the derivative \(1 - \frac{1}{x^2}\).
steps.insight: The order in the numerator matters: \(u'v - uv'\) (not \(uv' - u'v\)). The minus makes the difference.

steps.text: The chain rule for composite functions \(f(g(x))\): outer derivative times inner derivative.
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• \(\sin(x^2)\): outer \(\sin\), inner \(x^2\): \(\cos(x^2) \cdot 2x\)
• \((3x + 1)^5\): \(5(3x + 1)^4 \cdot 3 = 15(3x + 1)^4\)
• \(e^{-x^2}\): \(e^{-x^2} \cdot (-2x)\)
• \(\ln(2x + 1)\): \(\frac{1}{2x + 1} \cdot 2 = \frac{2}{2x + 1}\)
• \(\sqrt{x^2 + 1}\): \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} \cdot 2x = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}\)

The most common mistake is forgetting the inner derivative: \((\sin 3x)' = 3\cos 3x\), not \(\cos 3x\).

With several layers: differentiate from the outside in and multiply all factors. \((\sin^2(3x))' = 2\sin(3x) \cdot \cos(3x) \cdot 3\).
steps.insight: Ask yourself for every function: what is computed last? That is the outer function. Then apply the chain rule.

steps.text: The sign of the derivative reveals the behaviour of the function. The animation shows it for \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\): where \(f'\) is positive, \(f\) rises; where \(f'\) is negative, \(f\) falls.
steps.formula: f' > 0 \Rightarrow f \text{ rises}, \qquad f' < 0 \Rightarrow f \text{ falls}, \qquad f'(x_0) = 0 \Rightarrow \text{horizontal tangent}
steps.explanation:
Extrema are determined in two steps:
1. Necessary: \(f'(x_0) = 0\).
2. Sufficient: \(f'\) changes sign at \(x_0\), or \(f''(x_0) \neq 0\).
• \(f''(x_0) < 0\): local maximum
• \(f''(x_0) > 0\): local minimum

For \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\): \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1)\), so \(x = \pm 1\). \(f''(x) = 6x\): \(f''(-1) = -6 < 0\) ⇒ maximum \((-1, 2)\). \(f''(1) = 6 > 0\) ⇒ minimum \((1, -2)\).
steps.insight: \(f'(x_0) = 0\) alone is not enough: \(f(x) = x^3\) has a horizontal tangent at \(0\) but neither a maximum nor a minimum (saddle point).

steps.text: The second derivative describes curvature: how does the slope change?
steps.formula: f'' > 0: \text{convex (curving upwards)}, \qquad f'' < 0: \text{concave (curving downwards)}, \qquad f''(x_w) = 0 \text{ with sign change: inflection point}
steps.explanation:
An inflection point is where the curvature changes – the tangent "pierces" the graph. Necessary condition: \(f''(x_w) = 0\). Sufficient: \(f'''(x_w) \neq 0\) or a sign change of \(f''\).

For \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\): \(f''(x) = 6x = 0\) at \(x = 0\), \(f'''(0) = 6 \neq 0\) ⇒ inflection point \((0, 0)\) with slope \(f'(0) = -3\) (the steepest point between maximum and minimum).

The animation shows the tangents at the maximum, inflection point and minimum: horizontal, steepest, horizontal.
steps.insight: Inflection points are extrema of the FIRST derivative: there the slope is largest or smallest.

steps.text: A standard scheme for curve sketching. Example: \(f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x = x(x - 3)^2\).
steps.explanation:
1. Domain: \(\mathbb{R}\). Behaviour: \(x \to \infty\) gives \(+\infty\), \(x \to -\infty\) gives \(-\infty\) (odd degree, positive leading coefficient).
2. Roots: \(x(x - 3)^2 = 0\): \(x = 0\) (simple) and \(x = 3\) (double, the graph touches the axis).
3. Extrema: \(f' = 0\) at \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\). \(f''(1) = -6 < 0\): maximum \((1, 4)\). \(f''(3) = 6 > 0\): minimum \((3, 0)\).
4. Inflection point: \(f'' = 0\) at \(x = 2\), \(f(2) = 8 - 24 + 18 = 2\): inflection point \((2, 2)\).
5. Sketch: from bottom left through the origin up to the maximum \((1, 4)\), over the inflection point \((2, 2)\) down to the minimum \((3, 0)\), then up to the right again.

Check: the inflection point lies exactly midway between the two extrema: \(x = \frac{1 + 3}{2} = 2\) ✓ (true for cubic functions).
steps.insight: Always substitute into \(f\), not into \(f'\), to get the \(y\)-value: the extreme points have coordinates \((x_0, f(x_0))\).

steps.text: Optimisation problems: a quantity is to become maximal or minimal. Recipe: set up the objective function, substitute the constraint, differentiate, find the roots of the derivative, check the type.
steps.formula: \text{fence } 40\,\text{m, wall as one side:} \quad A(x) = x\,(40 - 2x), \quad A'(x) = 40 - 4x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 10
steps.explanation:
Example: a rectangle is fenced off with \(40\,\text{m}\) of fence against a house wall (the wall side needs no fence). What is the maximum area?

• Width \(x\) (two sides perpendicular to the wall), length \(y = 40 - 2x\).
• Objective function: \(A(x) = x(40 - 2x) = 40x - 2x^2\) for \(0 < x < 20\).
• \(A'(x) = 40 - 4x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 10\), \(y = 20\).
• \(A''(x) = -4 < 0\): maximum. \(A = 10 \cdot 20 = 200\,\text{m}^2\).

Check the boundary values: for \(x \to 0\) and \(x \to 20\), \(A\) tends to \(0\) – so the maximum lies inside ✓.
steps.insight: Don't forget the answer in a sentence: not just \(x = 10\), but also the wanted quantity \(200\,\text{m}^2\) and the second side \(20\,\text{m}\).

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. \(f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}\): slope of the tangent. Tangent: \(y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)\).

2. Power rule \((x^n)' = nx^{n-1}\), standard derivatives of \(e^x\), \(\ln x\), \(\sin x\), \(\cos x\).

3. Product rule \(u'v + uv'\), quotient rule \(\frac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}\), chain rule \(f'(g) \cdot g'\).

4. Extrema: \(f' = 0\) and \(f'' \neq 0\) (\(< 0\) maximum, \(> 0\) minimum). Inflection point: \(f'' = 0\), \(f''' \neq 0\).

5. Optimisation: objective function, constraint, differentiate, check type and boundary values.
steps.insight: Congratulations! In "Differential Calculus" you learn the formal definition, the mean value theorem and Taylor polynomials, in "Multidimensional Calculus" partial derivatives. The rules from here apply there unchanged.
